This laboratory-to-life gap is especially consequential when laboratory-derived mechanisms are used to explain clinically relevant processes that unfold in complex, dynamic environments.

By integrating laboratory and field methods within a single framework, researchers can determine whether psychological constructs operate consistently across settings and distinguish shared from contextspecific variation. In this multi-method approach, convergence strengthens evidence for the generalizability of the process across contexts, while divergence offers equally vital insights into contextual boundaries, measurement limitations, or both. This kind of laboratory-field integration is consistent with broader calls in behavioral science, such as the NIMH's Research Domain Criteria framework, which advocates for bridging methodologies with complementary strengths in order to more accurately characterize clinically relevant mechanisms. 1 We use alcohol administration as a high-fidelity model system for testing this cross-context generalizability. Alcohol intoxication offers a consistent, well-characterized state that can be experimentally manipulated in the laboratory and naturally observed in daily life, [2] [3] [4] making it particularly well suited for testing the laboratory-to-life gap. Acute psychological responses to alcohol (including stimulation, sedation, intoxication, and craving 5 ) have long been considered clinically informative candidate mechanisms of alcohol use disorder (AUD) risk. [6] [7] [8] [9] Variation in these responses may help explain why some individuals experience alcohol in ways that increase prospective risk for escalation to problematic use. [10] [11] [12] Because these responses can be assessed repeatedly in both controlled and naturalistic drinking episodes using identical instruments, they provide a rare opportunity to test whether individual differences in alcohol response reflect stable tendencies that generalize across contexts. If these alcohol response processes show similar patterns across laboratory and real-world drinking episodes, that would strengthen confidence that laboratory assessments capture meaningful person-level tendencies rather than artifacts of an artificial setting. If they do not, that too would be important, suggesting that acute alcohol responses are more context-sensitive than laboratory models alone would imply.

A useful way to frame this question is in terms of trajectories. Acute alcohol-response trajectories may be characterized by both their overall level and their pattern of change over the course of the drinking episode. Borrowing a simple metaphor, these two components can be thought of as the "volume" and "tempo" of alcohol response, respectively. Crucially, these trajectories are jointly defined by multiple parameters-including initial levels, rates of change, and in some cases, acceleration (i.e., quadratic effects)-which together characterize the predicted level of response at any given moment. An individual's average level of stimulation, sedation, intoxication, or craving may plausibly reflect a relatively stable sensitivity to alcohol that generalizes across contexts, whereas the pace and shape of change in those responses may be more contingent on contextual features, such as social interaction, drinking pace, beverage exposure, and the metric used to index progression through the episode. Thus, trajectories provide a useful framework for asking not only whether alcohol responses correspond across contexts, but also which specific components of those responses are most likely to generalize.

Despite the theoretical importance of this cross-context correspondence, empirical integration remains sparse. A major limitation of prior work is that the laboratory and real-world contexts used to study alcohol response differ in consequential ways. The vast majority of extant laboratory research (~90% 13 ) has relied heavily on solitary or otherwise asocial drinking protocols, even though real-world drinking commonly unfolds in social settings shaped by interpersonal, motivational, and contextual influences. 14, 15 At the same time, many large-scale studies of alcohol response have relied on retrospective self-reports, sometimes recalling experiences with alcohol that occurred years in the past, 10 even though retrospective reports correspond only modestly with in-the-moment experience and are vulnerable to recall bias. [16] [17] [18] Bringing laboratory alcohol administration together with in-the-moment EMA offers a rare opportunity to test whether the same alcohol response processes are observed across settings with complementary strengths.

To our knowledge, only four prior studies have paired laboratory and EMA alcohol response assessments within the same participants, and these investigations were restricted by small samples and design constraints that limited their ability to estimate person-level correspondence with precision. [19] [20] [21] [22] Moreover, these two approaches may diverge for principled reasons. As work integrating naturalistic and experimental methods in other domains has emphasized, 23 experimental paradigms reduce confounding and sharpen causal interpretation, whereas naturalistic assessments better capture the construal, selection, and evocation processes through which responses unfold in everyday life. In addition, even when normative trajectory patterns appear broadly similar across settings, the degree of person-level correspondence in specific trajectory parameters may still be modest, particularly when the forms of change being compared are not identical across contexts. In the alcohol domain, such differences are likely especially relevant for dynamic change, because average levels and rates of change may not be equally sensitive to contextual variation. The present study was designed to provide a stronger and more informative comparison between laboratory and daily-life alcohol responses. First, with N=282 heavy-drinking young adults, this study provides a substantially larger and more precise test than prior lab-EMA alcohol-response studies of person-level correspondence. Second, by employing a socially unscripted triadic (i.e., small-group) alcohol administration paradigm, we minimize the traditional ecological gap between laboratory drinking and real-world drinking. Third, we paired that laboratory session with intensive, event-contingent EMA sampling 24 during participants' naturalistic drinking episodes. Fourth, we assessed the same four domains of alcohol response across contexts using identical self-report measures at matching 30-minute intervals.

This design preserved the distinctive advantages of each assessment approach while achieving unusually high measurement alignment. Crucially, our framework allowed for principled divergence recognizing that standard dosing and self-paced drinking may yield distinct but related signatures. It also made it possible to examine normative trajectory patterns across contexts-including similarities or differences in average level, shape, and direction of change-as a meaningful part of the comparison rather than merely a backdrop for person-level correlations. The present study had three aims. First, we characterized and compared normative alcoholresponse trajectories across contexts. Establishing these mean-level benchmarks, such as whether participants experience higher peak intoxication in the laboratory versus daily life, is a necessary prerequisite for interpreting person-level correspondence. 25, 26 Second, we quantified person-level correspondence in "volume" (intercepts) to test whether average sensitivity generalizes across context.

Third, we determined the generalizability of "tempo" (slopes) to test whether individual differences in the pace of response are maintained across settings. Consistent with our preregistration, we expected some level of positive correspondence across contexts and used the present analyses to estimate the magnitude and uncertainty of those associations. Using preregistered multilevel structural equation modeling (MSEM), we evaluated correspondence in both trajectory components while accounting for measurement uncertainty. Evidence of convergence would support the view that laboratory and real-world assessments capture shared alcohol-response processes despite their contextual differences, whereas evidence of selective or limited convergence would help identify which components of alcohol response generalize most readily across settings. In either case, the findings provide an important benchmark for evaluating the generalizability of laboratory alcohol paradigms and, more broadly, for integrating experimental and naturalistic methods in the study of clinically relevant psychological mechanisms.

Results

Sample Characteristics and Descriptive Alcohol-Response Trajectories Across Contexts

The final analytic sample for our primary analyses included 282 participants who received alcohol during the laboratory session, of whom 278 (98.6%) also provided EMA data during naturalistic drinking episodes. In the laboratory, participants' mean BAC increased from zero at baseline (M=0.00, SD=0.00) to 0.060 (SD=0.016) post-drink, then continued to rise to 0.071 (SD=0.012) and 0.073 (SD=0.012) at the third and fourth timepoint respectively (see Figure 1). As shown in Figure 2, stimulation peaked at 30 minutes in the lab (M=55.1, SD=24.3) before declining at subsequent timepoints, exhibiting an inverted-U pattern. In contrast, sedation progressively increased from baseline (M=11.8, SD=14.6) to the final assessment (M=24.9, SD=22.1). Both subjective intoxication and craving were highest post-drink, followed by a gradual decrease across the session.

During the EMA protocol, participants reported an average of 7.77 drinking episodes (SD=3.98, range: 1-18), providing a mean of 31.72 observations per participant (SD=24.62, range: 1-126) and 4.08 observations per drinking episode (SD=2.77, range: 1-15). Cumulatively, this yielded a robust dataset of 8,818 total observations. Across these naturalistic drinking occasions, participants consumed an average of 5.33 drinks per episode (SD=3.63, range: 1-26). About 73% of drinking episodes began with a cumulative drink count of 1 (indicating that the participant initiated the survey at or near their first drink), while about 27% began with a cumulative count greater than 1 (indicating some drinks were consumed before the first survey was completed). Multiple drinking episodes on the same calendar day were rare (14 person-days across the entire sample). Estimated BAC during the first four EMA surveys within episodes (mirroring the time frame of the laboratory session) showed an ascending pattern (survey 1 M=0.048 (SD=0.030), survey 2 M=0.080 (SD=0.050), survey 3 M=0.107 (SD=0.065), survey 4 M=0.126 (SD=0.072)), indicating somewhat higher peak BAC values compared to the laboratory.

Figure 3 compares EMA-assessed alcohol responses with laboratory patterns. EMA stimulation (M=47.5, SD=17.0), on average, was comparable to mid-session laboratory levels, but it demonstrated substantial variability across the eBAC range compared to the lab. EMA sedation (M=14.3, SD=16.4) and intoxication (M=9.91, SD=7.85), on average, were generally lower than laboratory assessments at comparable BAC levels, while craving (M=14.3, SD=20.4), on average, was substantially lower in naturalistic settings compared to laboratory assessments. Although laboratory alcohol responses showed clear time-dependent patterns, EMA alcohol responses demonstrated considerable between-person and within-episode heterogeneity in eBAC-dependent patterns. Figure 4 displays the distribution of BAC/eBAC values across laboratory and EMA contexts, illustrating both the broader range and higher central tendency of eBAC values observed during naturalistic drinking compared to BAC during the more controlled laboratory alcohol administration.

Convergence Between Laboratory and EMA Alcohol Responses

The primary aim of this study was to determine whether individual differences in laboratoryassessed alcohol-response trajectories generalized to naturalistic drinking settings. Table 1 presents the complete parameter estimates from the Bayesian three-level models for each outcome. Because trajectories are jointly defined by both their overall level and their pattern of change, we examined crosscontext correspondence in both intercept and slope parameters. Accordingly, the table presents correlations between laboratory and EMA alcohol-response intercepts and slopes as complementary indicators of whether alcohol-response trajectories generalize across contexts. The table also presents the estimated intercepts and slopes in each setting, along with the full covariance structure among these person-level trajectory parameters. For each alcohol-response domain, we first describe the normative trajectories in the laboratory and EMA settings, as these provide essential context for interpreting the correspondence results. We then describe the correlations between lab and EMA intercepts and slopes, followed by other significant associations among trajectory parameters within each context. As preregistered, results from the first EMA burst are presented as the primary analysis, followed by a sensitivity analysis including all three EMA bursts. Figure 5 displays scatterplots illustrating the lab-EMA slope associations for each outcome, which we report alongside the corresponding intercept associations in Table 1. The posterior distributions for the per-participant random slopes can be found in the supplemental materials. As detailed below, across outcomes, a clear overall pattern emerged: laboratory and EMA intercepts showed positive correspondence for all four alcohol-response domains, indicating that individuals' average response levels (volume) were relatively similar across contexts. By contrast, evidence for slope (tempo) correspondence was more limited and outcome specific. Sedation showed the clearest evidence of positive lab-EMA slope correspondence, whereas slope associations for stimulation, intoxication, and craving were generally weaker and more uncertain. Thus, the main finding was not a simple validation or invalidation of laboratory alcohol paradigms, but a differentiation of which components of alcohol response generalized across contexts. We describe these overall patterns in detail below, beginning with the normative trajectories in the laboratory and EMA settings because similarities and differences in average level, shape, and direction of change across settings provide essential context for interpreting the person-level correspondence estimates.

Stimulation.

Laboratory stimulation responses showed an inverted-U pattern across time, peaking shortly after alcohol consumption ended (i.e., the post-drink assessment) before declining (mean linear slope at the midpoint of the curve =-3.01, 95% CI [-3.76, -2.23]; mean quadratic slope=-5.53, 95% CI [-6.53, -4.56]). EMA stimulation responses showed a modest average decrease across the modeled ascending-to-peak eBAC window (mean slope=-0.68, 95% CI [-0.78, -0.58]). Laboratory and EMA intercepts showed a positive correlation (r=0.42, 95% CI [0.27, 0.60]), indicating that participants with higher stimulation at the laboratory session midpoint also tended to report higher average stimulation levels across their naturalistic drinking episodes. In contrast, there was little evidence that individual differences in the laboratory linear slope (r=0.11, 95% CI [-0.26, 0.51]) or quadratic (r=-0.18, 95% CI [-0.48, 0.10]) slope corresponded with individual differences in EMA slope. The 95% credible intervals for both correlations were wide and encompassed values ranging from meaningful negative to meaningful positive associations. Sensitivity analyses including all three EMA bursts yielded similar null results (linear: r=0.02, 95% CI [-0.34, 0.38]; quadratic: r=-0.22, 95% CI [-0.52, 0.04]). Additionally, participants' average EMA stimulation levels (EMA intercept) were negatively correlated with their EMA slopes (r=-0.46, 95% CI [-0.73, -0.22]), indicating that individuals who reported higher average stimulation during naturalistic drinking showed smaller increases (or greater decreases) in stimulation as eBAC rose.

Sedation.

Both laboratory and EMA sedation responses showed positive trajectories, with sedation increasing as BAC rose in both contexts (lab mean linear slope at midpoint=4.88, 95% CI [3.99, 5.79]; lab mean quadratic slope=0.70, 95% CI [-0.05, 1.46]; EMA mean slope=0.45, 95% CI [0.35, 0.56]). Laboratory and EMA intercepts showed a positive correlation (r=0.54, 95% CI [0.38, 0.73]), indicating that participants with higher sedation at the laboratory session midpoint tended to also report higher average sedation levels during naturalistic drinking. Individual differences in the laboratory linear sedation slope were also positively correlated with individual differences in the EMA linear sedation slope (r=0.26, 95% CI [0.03, 0.50]), suggesting that participants who showed steeper laboratory sedation trajectories tended to also show steeper sedation trajectories during naturalistic drinking. The laboratory quadratic slope showed a negative correlation with EMA slopes (r=-0.36, 95% CI [-0.66, -0.08]), indicating that participants with more accelerating sedation trajectories in the lab showed less steep EMA sedation slopes, increasing less over naturalistic drinking sessions. The all-bursts sensitivity analysis showed similar patterns (linear: r=0.28, 95% CI [0.07, 0.51]; quadratic: r=-0.31, 95% CI [-0.59, -0.05]). Laboratory intercepts (average sedation) were positively correlated with laboratory linear slopes (r=0.64, 95% CI [0.47, 0.86]), indicating that participants reporting higher sedation at the session midpoint showed steeper increases over time. Similarly, average EMA sedation correlated positively with EMA slopes (r=0.52, 95% CI [0.31, 0.75]).

Intoxication.

Intoxication followed an inverted-U trajectory in the laboratory, peaking early in the session before declining, whereas intoxication increased with eBAC during naturalistic drinking (lab mean linear slope at the midpoint=9.10, 95% CI [8.38, 9.80]; lab mean quadratic slope=-10.51, 95% CI [-11.39, -9.65]; EMA mean slope=0.74, 95% CI [0.69, 0.80]). Laboratory and EMA intercepts showed a positive correlation (r=0.42, 95% CI [0.26, 0.61]), indicating that participants with higher intoxication at the laboratory session midpoint tended to report higher average intoxication levels during naturalistic drinking. Individual differences in the laboratory linear slope showed a small positive correlation with individual differences in the EMA slope (r=0.13, 95% CI [-0.06, 0.35]), though the credible interval included zero, indicating substantial uncertainty. The laboratory quadratic slope showed a negative but uncertain correlation with EMA slopes (r=-0.20, 95% CI [-0.50, 0.09]), indicating that participants with more accelerating intoxication trajectories in the lab showed less steep EMA intoxication slopes, increasing less over naturalistic drinking sessions. The all-bursts analysis yielded similar point estimates with slightly narrower credible intervals (linear: r=0.17, 95% CI [-0.00, 0.35]; quadratic: r=-0.27, 95% CI [-0.53, -0.02]).

The pattern of growth-factor correlations in the laboratory intoxication model helps clarify the trajectory as a whole. There was a near-perfect positive correlation between laboratory intercepts and linear slopes (r=0.94, 95% CI [0.77, 1.16]) and a near-perfect negative correlation with quadratic slopes (r = -0.93, 95% CI [-1.32, -0.61]). This indicates that participants' intoxication level at the midpoint was tightly linked to both how steeply intoxication was rising at that point and how sharply it declined thereafter, underscoring the extent to which the laboratory intoxication trajectory was jointly structured across parameters.

Craving.

Craving followed an inverted-U pattern in the laboratory, peaking shortly after alcohol consumption before declining, whereas craving decreased with eBAC during naturalistic drinking (lab mean linear slope=1.69, 95% CI [0.58, 2.77]; lab mean quadratic slope=-5.83, 95% CI [-6.88, -4.83]; EMA mean slope=-0.14, 95% CI [-0.19, -0.09]). Laboratory and EMA intercepts showed a positive correlation (r=0.48, 95% CI [0.33, 0.67]), indicating that participants with higher craving at the laboratory session midpoint tended to report higher average craving levels during naturalistic drinking. Individual differences in the laboratory linear slope showed a small positive correlation with individual differences in the EMA slope (r=0.28, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.61]), though the credible interval included zero, indicating substantial uncertainty. The laboratory quadratic slope showed a negative correlation with the EMA linear slope(r=-0.35, 95% CI [-0.65, -0.07]). The all-bursts analysis yielded nearly identical results (linear: r=0.28, 95% CI [0.01, 0.59]; quadratic: r=-0.31, 95% CI [-0.57, -0.07]).

Synthesis Across Outcomes.

As previewed above, a consistent pattern emerged across all four outcomes: laboratory and EMA intercepts showed positive correlations (r = .42 to .54), indicating that individuals' average response levels (volume) were similar across contexts. In contrast, the correlations between laboratory and EMA slopes tended to be weaker and more uncertain for many outcomes, suggesting limited convergence across contexts in how rapidly responses changed as a function of alcohol's effects (tempo). Sedation showed the clearest evidence of positive lab-EMA slope correspondence, whereas slope associations for stimulation, intoxication, and craving were generally weaker and more uncertain. The normative trajectories help contextualize this pattern. In several cases, mean-level trajectories were broadly similar across settings even when parameter-specific slope correspondence was weak or uncertain. Taken together, these findings indicate stronger cross-context convergence in overall response level than in the rate or form of within-episode change.

Figure 6 illustrates how laboratory parameters predict naturalistic drinking responses through the joint model's correlation structure, using stimulation as an example, given that it demonstrated the clearest quadratic trajectory in the laboratory. We created 27 simulated individuals representing systematic combinations of laboratory intercept, linear slope, and quadratic slope values (each set at -1 SD, mean, or +1 SD). For each simulated individual, we used the model's estimated correlations to calculate the expected EMA intercept and slope given their laboratory parameters. Each panel displays the observed laboratory trajectory alongside the predicted EMA trajectory for one simulated individual. The variation (or lack thereof) in predicted EMA trajectories across panels with different laboratory slope values reflects the strength of lab-EMA slope correlations, while variation across intercept levels reflects lab-EMA intercept correlations. Consistent with the primary analyses, the predicted EMA trajectories show substantial variation across panels differing in laboratory intercept values (columns), reflecting the moderate lab-EMA intercept correlations. In contrast, predicted EMA slopes remain relatively consistent across panels with different laboratory linear and quadratic slope values (rows and within columns), reflecting the weak and uncertain correlations between laboratory and EMA slopes. This pattern further illustrates that laboratory-derived differences in overall response level were more informative about naturalistic drinking responses than laboratory-derived differences in trajectory shape or rate of change.

Exploratory Analyses

Placebo participants demonstrated a similar pattern of limited lab-EMA slope convergence as the alcohol group (see Table S1), with sedation showing the only notable positive correlation (r=0.36, 95% CI [0.04, 0.74]), suggesting the obtained convergence results for reported sedation are not primarily driven by pharmacological effects. In addition, unlike the alcohol group, placebo participants did not show a clear positive association between laboratory and EMA intoxication intercepts, further suggesting that the cross-context correspondence in average intoxication levels was more specific to participants who received alcohol. As expected, the alcohol group showed substantially stronger laboratory responses than the placebo group, most notably for intoxication and sedation, confirming clear pharmacological effects beyond expectancy. The alcohol group also showed stronger associations between laboratory slopes and average EMA levels for sedation (r=0.44 vs. 0.12) and intoxication (r=0.38 vs. -0.04). However, this likely reflects range restriction rather than a substantive difference; with weaker laboratory responses in the placebo group, there is less variance in slopes to predict naturalistic outcomes.

Exploratory Follow-up Analyses that Were Not Preregistered

Due to the wide credible intervals observed for the primary lab-EMA slope correlations, coupled with the substantial heterogeneity in naturalistic drinking contexts compared to standardized laboratory conditions, we decided to perform several post-hoc descriptive analyses examining how EMA alcohol response slopes varied across contextual features. Unlike laboratory sessions, which followed a standardized protocol with controlled alcohol administration and consistent social context, naturalistic drinking episodes varied widely in peak eBAC and context. To better understand this heterogeneity and contextualize the primary findings, we conducted seven descriptive comparisons examining EMA slopes across: (1) number of EMA observations per episode (3, 4, or 5+ assessments), (2) peak eBAC (low <0.05 g/dL vs. lab-like 0.05-0.12 g/dL vs. high >0.12 g/dL), (3) social context (alone vs. with others), (4) group size for social episodes (1-2 vs. 3+ people), (5) type of drinking companions (alone vs. friends vs. partner/family vs. other), (6) drinking location (home vs. someone's home vs. bar/restaurant vs. other), and (7) same-day cannabis use (yes vs. no). These analyses are purely descriptive (see plots in Supplementary Materials); no statistical tests were conducted. All EMA slopes are reported as change per 0.01 g/dL increase in eBAC.

As expected, episodes with more EMA observations yielded more precise slope estimates with reduced variability (e.g., sedation slopes: 3 observations SD=4.81 vs. 5+ observations SD= .72), confirming that denser within-episode sampling improves measurement reliability. Peak eBAC and social and contextual factors showed minimal differentiation. Slopes were nearly identical for solitary versus social drinking across all outcomes (M differences <0.2 for all outcomes). Among social episodes, group size (1-2 vs. 3+ people) showed no meaningful differences. Companion type revealed one modest pattern: drinking with partner/family was associated with slightly steeper negative stimulation slopes (M=-2.23) compared to friends (M=-1.63) or drinking alone (M=-1.64), though distributions overlapped considerably. Drinking location showed no clear patterns, with similar mean slopes across home, bars/restaurants, and other venues for all outcomes (M differences <0.4). Same-day cannabis use (n=132 episodes) yielded similar slopes to cannabis-free episodes across all outcomes, though the limited sample precludes strong conclusions.

Because the associations between lower-order growth model parameters (e.g., linear slopes) in polynomial growth models can vary depending on the location of the intercept, 27 we conducted a final unregistered exploratory analysis where we re-centered the growth curve models so that the intercept was centered at the beginning of the drinking episode (at Time 1 for the laboratory sessions, and when eBAC was estimated to be at zero). These results may be found in the Supplemental Materials. Because recentering is most informative for the lower-order parameters, we focus on how the cross-context associations for the intercepts and linear slopes changed when the models were centered at the start of the drinking episode. Uncertainty was still high across all effects. Associations among intercepts were largely similar (e.g. within r = .10) except with intoxication. When the intercept was at the beginning of drinking, the level of intoxication was not correlated across lab and EMA (r = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.17, 0.30].

On the other hand, associations of the instantaneous linear slope in the lab (e.g. the linear slope at the intercept, or how quickly participants initially changed on craving, intoxication, sedation, and stimulation) with the linear slope in EMA (e.g. the linear rate of change across the drinking episode) were universally stronger for all variables, with credible intervals excluding zero for intoxication (r = 0.26, 95% CI [0.06, 0.48], sedation (r = 0.46, 95% CI [0.19, 0.76), and craving (r = 0.35, 95% CI [0.12, 0.61]; although stimulation was larger (r = 0.17, 95% CI [-0.09, 0.44], its credible interval did not exclude zero. In other words, how quickly participants reported change in most outcomes in the lab was modestly to strongly associated with change in real-world situations when we examined the rate of change at the start of the drinking episode, although these associations were estimated with a great deal of uncertainty. Figure 7 illustrates these results.

Discussion

A central challenge for psychological science is determining whether processes measured under controlled laboratory conditions generalize to the complex environments of daily life. The present study addressed this question in the domain of acute alcohol response by pairing an unscripted social laboratory alcohol-administration paradigm with intensive, event-contingent EMA in a large sample of heavydrinking young adults. The clearest pattern was that individual differences in overall response level corresponded across contexts in all four domains we examined, although the corresponding intercepts did not represent identical physical moments: the laboratory intercept indexed the centered laboratory drinking window, whereas the EMA intercept indexed average response across ascending-to-peak naturalistic observations. In contrast, correspondence in within-episode rate of change was weaker and more selective. Sedation showed the clearest evidence of positive slope correspondence across contexts, whereas slope associations for stimulation, intoxication, and craving were generally smaller and more uncertain. This distinction matters because it clarifies what laboratory paradigms may capture more reliably about real-world alcohol response. Individuals' overall response "volume" generalized more clearly across settings than the "tempo" or form of within-episode change, although unregistered exploratory analyses suggested that these associations also depended on centering decisions within drinking episodes.

An important contribution of this study is that it treats normative trajectories as substantively meaningful rather than merely preliminary to the person-level correspondence analyses. Mean-level patterns across settings helped contextualize the cross-context associations. For example, stimulation showed relatively similar average levels across laboratory and EMA contexts, suggesting that overall stimulation may generalize reasonably well across settings even when its within-episode dynamics are more variable in daily life. By contrast, sedation and intoxication were lower on average in EMA than in the laboratory, which may reflect the fact that the laboratory protocol imposed a standardized dose and timing structure that produced a more uniform, time-locked, and in some domains subjectively stronger alcohol-exposure window than the self-paced episodes captured by EMA. Craving was also lower on average in EMA than in the laboratory, perhaps because the laboratory pacing and constrained administration period made desire for additional alcohol especially salient at the assessment point, whereas participants in daily life could regulate their own pace and continue drinking more flexibly. The trajectories also differed in how closely their patterns of change aligned across settings, with sedation showing the most comparable directional pattern. These descriptive patterns matter because associations across assessment contexts cannot be interpreted in isolation from the broader trajectory it is meant to represent. More generally, the present findings underscore that strong person-level correspondence is not required for trajectories across settings to be informative, nor do broadly similar normative trajectories guarantee strong parameter-specific associations. Moreover, because decisions about the placement of the intercept influence associations among lower-order parameters in growth models, 27 it is critical to consider how considering both levels of analysis (i.e., normative trajectory patterns and person-level correspondence) provides a fuller picture of what does and does not generalize across laboratory and naturalistic drinking contexts. Sedation emerged as the clearest example of cross-context correspondence in both average levels and within-episode change. Participants who showed higher average sedation in the laboratory also tended to report higher average sedation during naturalistic drinking, and participants who showed steeper laboratory sedation trajectories also tended to show steeper EMA sedation trajectories. While subjective experiences of intoxication, stimulation, and craving are often heavily modulated by social environment, expectancy, and drinking pacing (ranging from gradual consumption to high intensity "pre-gaming" observed in naturalistic settings), 19, 28, 29 sedation may be less sensitive to contextual variation and more closely tied to alcohol's depressant effects than some other response domains. At the same time, the placebo analyses complicate a purely pharmacological interpretation, as placebo participants also showed a notable positive lab-EMA slope association for sedation. Thus, the relative robustness of sedation may reflect a combination of pharmacological sensitivity, expectancy-related processes, or both. Rather than supporting a simple conclusion that sedation is a uniquely pure marker of alcohol's pharmacological effects, the findings suggest that sedation may be a domain in which cross-context correspondence is comparatively easier to detect, even if the sources of that correspondence are not exclusively pharmacological.

In contrast to the relative robustness of the sedation findings, stimulation, intoxication, and craving-domains widely considered central to ascending-limb risk [30] [31] [32] -showed a more complex pattern of generalizability across contexts. For all three domains, average response levels ("volume") showed positive cross-context correspondence, indicating that individuals' relative standing on these responses generalized across settings. By contrast, within-episode change ("tempo") was less consistent, although exploratory analyses suggested that this depended on the placement of the intercept. For stimulation, slope correspondence was weak and uncertain despite a clear positive intercept association. For intoxication and craving, slope estimates were somewhat more suggestive but still less robust than the corresponding intercept associations. This pattern suggests that average response levels and dynamic changes may differ in how readily they generalize across contexts. A person's typical level of stimulation, intoxication, or craving may reflect a relatively stable tendency that carries from the laboratory into daily life, whereas the pace and form of change in those responses may be more contingent on idiosyncratic variation in beverage choice, drinking pace, episode structure, social context, and the timing of assessment. In the laboratory, the rapid, standardized administration of alcohol under controlled conditions likely produced a more time-locked rise in intoxication, stimulation, and craving than is typical of naturalistic drinking episodes. Taken together, these findings suggest that overall response level in these domains generalizes more clearly across contexts than the dynamic unfolding of response over the course of drinking.

An additional interpretive issue is that correspondence involving laboratory slope parameters depends in part on where the curvilinear laboratory trajectory is centered. This is not merely a technical caveat, rather it helps clarify when laboratory and real-world alcohol responses are most comparable. In the primary analyses, laboratory slopes were centered at the midpoint of the drinking episode, which provides one estimate of instantaneous change at that point, but may not map equally well onto the EMA slope for all outcomes. This issue is especially relevant for outcomes such as stimulation and intoxication, where the laboratory trajectories showed pronounced curvature and the EMA slopes indexed change over a somewhat different portion of the drinking episode. That is, it is important to remember that for curvilinear alcohol-response trajectories, linear slope parameter correspondence depends not only on whether slopes are compared across contexts, but also on where along the response curve those slopes are defined for the curvilinear trajectory (i.e., the lab trajectory). We therefore conducted a post hoc recentering analysis in which the laboratory linear slope was evaluated at the start of the drinking episode, thereby indexing early response change rather than midpoint rate of change. These analyses suggested stronger lab-EMA slope correspondence when laboratory change was defined early in the response curve.

If comparing the all-bursts models, lab-EMA slope correlations increased from .28 to .46 for sedation, .02 to .17 for stimulation, .17 to .26 for intoxication, and .28 to .35 for craving. These shifts suggest that the earliest portion of the alcohol response curve may carry the clearest person-level signal across laboratory and real-world contexts, before naturalistic drinking episodes diverge through self-pacing, beverage choice, mobility, social selection, and continued drinking decisions. Thus, the weaker midpoint slope findings should not be interpreted as evidence that dynamic alcohol response processes fail to generalize. Rather, they indicate that cross-context generalizability depends on which phase of the dynamic process is being compared.

Notably, the same issue is at play for the intercepts, and in our post hoc exploratory analyses we found that intercept location (shifting to start of trajectory from midpoint) mattered a great deal for intoxication, and less so for other variables. Specifically, the intoxication intercept association was much weaker at the start of the trajectories, r = .06, 95% CI [-.17, .30], than when it was evaluated at the midpoint, r = .42, 95% CI [.26, .61] in the primary model. This pattern argues against the interpretation that lab-EMA correspondence simply reflects a generic tendency to endorse higher subjective response items. Instead, correspondence appears to depend on where in the drinking episode the response is indexed, suggesting meaningful temporal specificity.

These results therefore support a view of laboratory and naturalistic methods as complementary rather than hierarchical. The present study does not suggest that the laboratory is simply validated only when it perfectly agrees with EMA, nor that EMA should be treated as the unquestioned criterion. Instead, each approach provides access to different strengths. Laboratory paradigms permit standardized alcohol exposure, common timing structures, and strong internal control, whereas EMA captures experience as it unfolds in real-world drinking episodes shaped by social, behavioral, and contextual variability. The most informative conclusion is not that one method substitutes for the other, but that some components of alcohol-response trajectories, particularly average response levels, show clearer cross-context correspondence than others, and that there may be periods of the process (early vs. late) that show higher correspondence. The central question is therefore not whether one method is "right," but which components of alcohol response each method captures best. Framed more broadly, this pattern is relevant beyond alcohol research, as it suggests that laboratory-to-life generalizability in behavioral science may depend not only on the construct being studied, but also on which component of that construct is being compared across settings.

The exploratory follow-up analyses further support this interpretation. Measured contextual features of EMA drinking episodes did not strongly differentiate alcohol-response slopes, but denser within-episode sampling was associated with more precise estimates and reduced variability. This pattern suggests that at least some of the uncertainty surrounding slope correspondence may reflect the greater difficulty of estimating dynamic change under naturalistic conditions rather than the absence of any shared underlying process. In other words, weaker slope convergence may arise in part because withinepisode change is harder to measure precisely in daily life, especially when drinking is self-paced and assessments occur at fixed intervals that may not align perfectly with the steepest changes in subjective response. Though results also suggest early in the process the two contexts produce more similar responses.

These findings point to several priorities for future work. One is to increase ecological symmetry between laboratory and field protocols when the goal is to compare dynamic trajectories. In the present study, laboratory participants received a standardized dose under a structured timing schedule while remaining seated, whereas naturalistic drinking episodes were self-paced and unfolded under less constrained behavioral and contextual conditions. Thus, weaker correspondence in within-episode change may reflect not only measurement limitations, but also the greater physicality, agency, and iterative decision-making inherent in real-world drinking, including ongoing choices about what to drink, how much to drink, how quickly to drink, and how to respond to shifting social cues. Future work could test whether more ecologically flexible laboratory designs, including self-administration paradigms, greater physical mobility, or opportunities to move through changing social environments, improve cross-context correspondence in dynamic alcohol-response trajectories. Continuous transdermal alcohol sensing, 33 denser EMA prompts, or adaptive sampling around moments of rapid change may also be especially useful for clarifying whether weaker slope correspondence reflects contextual divergence, measurement limitations, or both. More broadly, laboratory protocols that better approximate the physical and volitional features of naturalistic drinking may help clarify how overall response level and within-episode change generalize across settings.

A second priority is to identify stable individual-difference factors that shape alcohol-response trajectories across settings. Although average response levels generalized more strongly than withinepisode slopes, there was substantial person-level variation in both components. Future work should test whether factors such as alcohol-related problems, drinking motives, or personality traits help explain who shows stronger correspondence across contexts and under what conditions. 29 Such work may be particularly informative for the more dynamic components of alcohol response, where context dependence appears greater and unexplained heterogeneity remains substantial. From a clinical perspective, clarifying which risk profiles are associated with higher field intercepts or steeper response slopes could help identify the contexts in which alcohol-related risk is most likely to emerge. For example, if individuals higher in trait extraversion show more persistent stimulation in social drinking environments, that information could help refine just-in-time adaptive interventions aimed at high-risk social contexts. 34 Several limitations should also be noted. First, the present analyses focused on four alcoholresponse domains, leaving out other potentially important dimensions of the drinking experience. Future research should evaluate whether similar patterns emerge for other response domains, including those more closely tied to emotional reinforcement, such as increases in positive emotions and/or decreases negative emotions, 5 especially since greater emotional reinforcement in lab settings predicts increased alcohol-related problems. 12, 31 Second, although the 30-minute EMA interval provided relatively dense sampling for field research, it may still have been insufficient to capture rapid changes in subjective response during naturalistic drinking episodes, particularly for slope estimation. Unlike the laboratory, where alcohol consumption was tightly linked to the assessment schedule, naturalistic drinking pace was idiosyncratic; as a result, fixed 30-minute EMA prompts may not always have aligned with an individual's peak intoxication or steepest rise in response. This mismatch in capture timing may have contributed to the measurement noise surrounding slope estimates and, in turn, to weaker slope correspondence across contexts. Third, the laboratory and EMA trajectory forms were not identical, which necessarily complicates direct parameter comparison even when the measures and timing structure are closely aligned. More generally, for outcomes with curvilinear laboratory trajectories, the interpretation of lab-EMA slope correspondence is sensitive to centering decisions, because the meaning of the laboratory linear slope changes across the drinking episode. At the same time, although using identical self-report measures across laboratory and EMA contexts was a strength because it maximized construct comparability for subjective alcohol responses, reliance on the same method in both settings may also have introduced shared-method variance that could inflate some cross-context associations. That concern is somewhat reduced, however, by the fact that associations were domain-specific, differed across alcohol and placebo groups, and varied meaningfully as a function of centering decisions. Thus, the correspondence observed here is unlikely to reflect shared response style alone, but future studies would benefit from including behavioral, physiological, or passive-sensing indicators of alcohol response alongside self-report. Finally, the sample consisted of heavy-drinking young adults, and the extent to which these findings generalize to lighter drinkers, older adults, or individuals with more chronic alcoholrelated problems remains to be established. This limitation is especially relevant because heavy-drinking young adults may have more practiced drinking routines, higher tolerance, and more frequent social drinking contexts than other populations.

Conclusions

The present findings provide a benchmark for evaluating what laboratory alcohol-administration paradigms do, and do not, capture about alcohol response in daily life. Across all four domains, laboratory and EMA assessments showed positive correspondence in average response level, indicating that overall response "volume" generalized more clearly across settings than within-episode "tempo." Correspondence in dynamic change was more selective, with sedation showing the clearest evidence of slope generalizability. More broadly, these results support the view that laboratory and naturalistic methods offer complementary insights into alcohol-response processes. For psychological science more generally, the findings suggest that laboratory-to-life generalizability should be evaluated at the level of specific dynamic components-levels, slopes, timing, and context-rather than treated as an all-or-none property of a paradigm.

Materials and Methods

Open Practices Statement

The study reported in this article was part of a preregistered NIH-funded clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier NCT03467191). For the current paper, the preregistered aims, hypotheses, and data analytic plan, along with the data, analysis code, and analysis results are publicly available https://osf.io/rv39t/.

Participants

This study draws from a previously described study sample of 393 heavy-drinking young adults (ages 21-29; 50% female), who participated in a multiparticipant alcohol administration study and were randomly assigned to consume alcoholic or placebo beverages. 35 Participants were recruited from the Pittsburgh metropolitan area via online advertisements, community flyers, and the University of Pittsburgh's Clinical Translational Science Institute (CTSI) Research Participant Registry. The CTSI Registry is a database of people interested in participating in research that matches potential participants to studies. Inclusion criteria were: age 21-29, ownership of a smartphone, drinking at least once per week, binge drinking (4+/5+ drinks for women/men) on at least four occasions in the past month, and ability to consume at least three drinks in 30 minutes. Exclusion criteria included current or past treatment for alcohol/substance use disorder, diagnosis of moderate/severe AUD or serious psychiatric disorders (e.g., schizophrenia, bipolar disorder), non-English speaking, ineligibility for the protocol's sex-based alcoholdosing algorithm, and contraindications for alcohol consumption (e.g., prior adverse reactions, pregnancy, medical conditions, disqualifying medications, or BMI <18.5 or >29.9).

Procedure Overview

This study was approved by the Carnegie Mellon University Institutional Review Board. All participants completed the laboratory alcohol administration session, and 389 participants completed the EMA burst, which began as soon as possible after the drinking session (e.g., the following weekend).

During the lab session, participants consumed either a placebo beverage or alcohol (randomly assigned) in triads (groups of three strangers) to simulate a more ecologically valid social drinking context. Following the lab visit, all participants engaged in real-time EMA assessments of their alcohol responses during naturally occurring drinking episodes over two long weekends (Thursday through Sunday). Identical selfreport items were administered at multiple timepoints across both contexts, allowing for direct comparison of subjective alcohol responses. Participants also completed similar EMA bursts at 6-and 12months post-laboratory session.

Laboratory Alcohol Administration Session

Participants were randomly assigned to groups of three unacquainted individuals and to beverage condition (alcohol or placebo; 2.4:1 allocation). Participants arrived at the lab after fasting for four hours and abstaining from alcohol for at least 24 hours. After baseline assessments and confirmation of sobriety (BAC = 0.00%), participants consumed their beverages during a 36-minute period around a circular table where triad members were permitted to interact naturally (see 35 for more details). To encourage spontaneous, naturalistic interaction, participants were told they were seated together to facilitate drink administration and communication with the experimenter prior to the study tasks, and no instructions were given about how or whether to interact with one another (other than not to discuss how intoxicated they might be feeling). All groups interacted across the 36-minute group drinking period. Alcohol groups consumed a standardized cranberry-vodka cocktail (alcohol dose: 0.82 g/kg for men, 0.74 g/kg for women), while placebo groups received flattened tonic water (poured from a vodka bottle) and cranberry juice cocktail, including vodka-rimmed glasses and false BAC readings. Placebo deception was achieved for all but one participant.

Subjective responses to alcohol were assessed at four timepoints at baseline and on the ascending limb of the BAC curve: pre-drink (baseline), immediately post-drink, 30 minutes post-drink, and 60 minutes post-drink. At each timepoint, participants privately completed computer-based questionnaires measuring intoxication, stimulation, sedation, and craving (as described in Measures below). BAC recordings were also taken at these same time points.

EMA Procedure

Following completion of the laboratory session, all participants (both alcohol and placebo) began a smartphone-based EMA protocol to capture real-world subjective responses to alcohol that mirrored our lab-based assessments. Prior to initiating EMA, participants attended an in-person training session conducted by research staff in the laboratory, during which they were familiarized with the EMA procedures and received hands-on instruction in using the MetricWire platform (MetricWire Inc., Waterloo, ON, Canada) on their personal smartphones. During training, staff emphasized the importance of capturing high-quality, in-the-moment data during drinking episodes and helped participants anticipate when they were most likely to drink over the upcoming two weekends. The goal was to promote proactive engagement with the EMA protocol and minimize missed assessments.

EMA data were collected over two consecutive long weekends (Thursday to Sunday), beginning as soon as possible after the lab session. Participants were instructed to initiate a drinking episode report as soon as they finished consuming their first alcoholic drink (we also prompted participants during the evening hours to remind them to initiate these surveys if they were drinking alcohol), and to complete additional surveys every 30 minutes. Follow-up surveys were administered for a total of 6 hours, each remaining open for 10 minutes, with no stopping rule applied. These follow-up surveys were designed to capture the number of standard alcohol drinks consumed since the last survey, the drinking context (i.e., with others vs. alone), and acute, in-the-moment subjective responses to alcohol on the ascending limb of the BAC curve, paralleling the lab protocol. Surveys were brief and optimized for mobile delivery, with clear instructions and time stamps to encourage compliance. Two additional EMA bursts occurred at 6months and 12-months post-lab session.

Participants received regular reminders and guidance from research staff throughout the EMA protocol period, including encouragement to initiate surveys promptly at the start of drinking episodes and to maintain regular survey completion throughout the drinking episode. Research staff monitored compliance daily via the MetricWire dashboard. In cases of notable missingness, staff initiated discretionary contact to provide reminders or technical support, with the frequency and nature of outreach adapted to individual adherence patterns. Participants were compensated on a sliding scale based on the proportion of surveys completed, with bonuses for high adherence, consistent with best practices for incentivizing compliance in EMA research. This intensive, real-time data collection strategy, which is grounded in validated EMA methodology, enabled the collection of ecologically valid, within-person reports of subjective alcohol responses as they occurred in daily life.

Measures

Demographics.

As part of the baseline session, participants reported their sex, weight, age, race and ethnicity, and highest level of education achieved in years as a proxy for SES.

Alcohol Response.

Key domains of subjective alcohol response were assessed in both lab and EMA contexts, adapted from validated scales and consistent with prior research. 2, 9 Responses to all items were on a sliding scale from 0 (not at all) to 100 (extremely). To assess intoxication, participants were asked, "How intoxicated do you feel right now?". 30 The brief Biphasic Alcohol Effects Scale (BAES 36, 37 ) was used to assess alcohol's acute stimulant (elated, energized, excited, stimulated, talkative, up, vigorous) and sedative (difficulty concentrating, down, heavy head, inactive, sedated, slow thoughts, sluggish) effects.

The full 14-item scale was used in the lab; a brief 6-item scale was used during EMA assessments (energized, excited, up; sedated, slow thoughts, sluggish). 38 At all assessment time points, we modified the original BAES instructions to ask about current feelings ("How are you feeling right now?") rather than effects attributable to alcohol. 31 Finally, participants reported their current level of craving to drink alcohol by responding to one item previously found to have the largest factor loading on a 'craving/motivation' factor of SRA in a sample of heavy drinking young adults. 5, 31 Participants were asked, "Would you like to drink more alcohol right now?".

Internal consistency of the brief BAES stimulation and sedation subscales (3 items each) was adequate across all laboratory timepoints (Cronbach's α = .78-.94; McDonald's ω = .79-.94). For the EMA data, we calculated multilevel reliability, which decomposes variance across persons, time, and items.

Both subscales demonstrated strong reliability of between-person differences averaged over time (stimulation RkRn = .93; sedation RkRn = .93) and adequate reliability of within-person change averaged over items (stimulation Rcn = .76; sedation Rcn = .75).

Context.

For each EMA survey, participants were asked, "Are you with others?" with the following response options: "Yes, at least one other person is present"; "No, I'm alone."

Number of Alcoholic Drinks.

When participants initiated an EMA survey to indicate they began drinking, they were asked: "How many drinks have you had so far today?" At subsequent surveys delivered during the same drinking episode, participants were asked: "Since your last survey entry, how many drinks have you had?" Participants were trained in the lab to recognize standard drink sizes using actual glassware (e.g., a 12-ounce glass of beer) and were reminded to apply these standard drink definitions when completing the EMA surveys.

Estimated BAC (eBAC) calculation for EMA Data. At each EMA survey, we calculated eBAC using standard procedures. 39 We used participant-reported drinking data and precise time-stamped survey metadata, following validated procedures grounded in Widmark-based formulas. 40 The start of each drinking episode was identified based on participants' report of completing their first alcohol drink, which served as the reference point for calculating time elapsed during the drinking episode. At each subsequent EMA survey completed during the same episode, participants reported the number of standard drinks they had consumed since the last survey. The timing of each EMA entry was automatically captured by the smartphone-based survey software, allowing us to compute the number of minutes that had passed since drinking onset for each report. These time and drink quantity data were used to compute eBAC using the standard Widmark formula: 40 eBAC = [(N_drinks × 14 g) / (body_weight_g × r)] × 100 -(β₆₀ × hours) where N_drinks is the cumulative number of standard drinks reported since the start of the episode, body_weight_g is the participant's self-reported body weight (converted from pounds to grams; × 453.592), r is the Widmark constant (0.68 for males, 0.55 for females, consistent with Watson et al., 1981), and β₆₀ is the assumed constant elimination rate of 0.017 g/dL per hour.

One standard alcoholic drink was defined as containing 14 grams of pure alcohol. Time elapsed since drinking onset (hours) was calculated as the difference between each survey's timestamp and the timestamp of the first survey in that episode. Because the first survey was completed after the participant reported finishing their first drink, zero elapsed time was assigned to the first observation for the purposes of metabolism estimation. This approach uses time-stamped survey metadata rather than retrospective estimates of when drinking began.

Negative eBAC values (which can arise when estimated metabolism exceeds estimated absorption) were floored at zero. All calculations were automated using survey timestamps to ensure accuracy and minimize recall bias. This procedure enabled continuous modeling of estimated intoxication levels during naturalistic drinking episodes.

Data Analysis

Consistent with our preregistration, analyses were conducted using R for data preparation and Mplus for MSEM. To guide our analytical approach, we assumed that alcohol consumption influences subjective responses via its effects on BAC, recognizing that this process unfolds over time due to absorption kinetics. Ideally, we would have liked to estimate slopes for the association between BAC/(e)BAC and outcomes in both laboratory and EMA data, as this directly captures individual differences in how alcohol responses change as alcohol exposure increases over time. However, the structural differences between our lab and EMA data required an alternative approach. Specifically, in EMA, we directly modeled the association between eBAC and outcomes within each episode (Level 1), allowed these slopes to vary between episodes within persons (Level 2), and estimated person-level slopes as the average across all episodes (Level 3). In the laboratory, the single-episode drinking design precluded the use of an equivalent three-level random effects structure. However, because participants received a standardized alcohol dose with assessments at fixed intervals, time functioned as a reliable and valid proxy for BAC in these analyses. We therefore modeled lab-based alcohol responses using latent growth curve analysis, with time centered at the midpoint (i.e., between assessments 2 and 3). Together, these modeling strategies allowed us to estimate person-level alcohol-response trajectories in each context, including both overall levels of response and patterns of change over the course of the drinking episode. This approach allowed us to examine cross-context correspondence in complementary trajectory components-intercepts and slopes-while accommodating the different structural features of the laboratory and EMA data.

Primary Analyses.

We estimated the correlation between individual differences in laboratorybased and EMA-based per-participant alcohol response trajectories (i.e., intercepts and slopes) using a three-level Bayesian MSEM. This framework allowed us to jointly estimate the person-level alcohol response trajectories in both contexts and their correlation in a single step. Although we developed a contingency strategy to address potential convergence issues arising from the structural differences between the datasets (see pre-registration), the full three-level model successfully converged for all outcomes. This allowed us to interpret the primary model without modification. To ensure meaningful comparison with real-world drinking, primary analyses focused on the 282 participants who received an intoxicating dose in the laboratory. We further restricted the EMA data to the first burst to prioritize temporal proximity to the lab session. Finally, to better account for the curvilinear patterns we observed during visual inspection of the data, we modified the preregistered model to include a quadratic slope growth factor for the laboratory estimates so that laboratory trajectories could more accurately reflect the observed shape of change over time (quadratic growth did not improve model fit for the EMA data).

Inference Criteria.

Given the absence of prior data to inform expected effect sizes, we inferred convergence between the lab and EMA alcohol responses based on the precision of the estimates. We considered the association robust if the 95% credible interval (CI) for the correlation between the random intercepts and slopes excluded 0, respectively. We report and interpret effect sizes and uncertainty estimates for all findings.

Sensitivity and Exploratory Analyses.

We conducted two additional sets of analyses to evaluate the robustness of our findings. First, as a sensitivity analysis, we repeated the primary models using data from all three EMA bursts, rather than restricting the window to the first EMA burst, to test whether the results remained consistent across a longer timeframe. Second, we performed an exploratory analysis with participants in the laboratory placebo condition, which allowed us to test the specificity of lab-EMA correspondence in a context driven by expectancy effects rather than pharmacological effects.

Data Exclusions.

To ensure comparability with the laboratory protocol (which targeted the absorption phase/ascending limb), we restricted EMA analyses to the ascending limb of BAC of each drinking episode. Specifically, we identified the survey with the highest calculated eBAC in each episode as the peak. All surveys occurring prior to or at this peak were retained, while those occurring after the peak were classified as the descending limb of BAC and excluded. This approach allowed us to capture alcohol's ascending and peak effects in the naturalistic setting, mirroring the standardized laboratory dosing protocol. During data quality control, we identified instances where participant-reported number of drinks consumed yielded physiologically implausible eBAC estimates. Thus, prior to conducting primary analyses (though subsequent to preregistration), we excluded EMA observations where eBAC exceeded .35%. This resulted in the exclusion of 365 (3.9%) observations. One placebo participant correctly identified the absence of alcohol in their beverage in the lab. Consistent with our preregistered plan to differentiate between the pharmacological effects vs. expectancy effects of alcohol, this participant and their associated group members were excluded from placebo-focused analyses.

If there are things we can improve, please email us at metacheck@scienceverse.org or leave an issue at github.com/scienceverse/metacheck/issues.
